rail_guard.text: Dingle's railway closed in 1953 and the sheep have been using the track since. There's no train here, and I'm not entitled to sell you a ticket for one.
I'm the guard of nothing, to be honest. It's a lovely job. I get to wave at the bus.

boat_skipper.text: I run the dolphin trips. Fungie was in the harbour from 1983 until 2020. He greeted thirty-seven years of boats, and then he just quit.
We still go out and look. You don't give up on a friend. You only cross-check the tide table.

irish_teacher.text: Dingle's a Gaeltacht, so Irish is the everyday language. You'll hear it in the shop queue. 'Dia duit' is hello, and 'Dia is Muire duit' is the reply.
'Slán' is goodbye. 'Go raibh maith agat' is thank you. Say it badly and they'll love you for trying.

chipper_owner.text: The best fish supper in Ireland is whichever one you're eating hungry, standing in the wind, with the seagull watching.
We get the fish off the boats at eight. By nine they're gone. By ten I'm just telling people about it.

ceili_dancer.text: The set dances here go back to the quadrilles of old France. We changed them. Of course we did.
Arms straight, feet quick, and never look at your feet. If you look at your feet, the floor knows.

oceanworld_guide.text: Our aquarium has a tunnel with sharks overhead, and a tank of rays that behave like kids at a bus window.
The Blasket Islands are across the water. The last islanders left in 1953. They wrote beautiful books about it, in Irish.

gallarus_walker.text: Gallarus Oratory is a little dry-stone church shaped like an upturned boat, about twelve hundred years old. And it's still dry inside.
No mortar. Just stones that fit. It's the best bit of Irish engineering that nobody asked for.
